title: Bug Report Example: How to Write One That Gets Fixed
description: A complete bug report example, a copy-ready template, severity vs priority with clear examples, and the matching fields in Jira and Azure DevOps.
excerpt: A vague bug report sits in the backlog. A precise one gets reproduced on the first try. Here is a complete example, a template to copy, and the same fields in Jira and Azure DevOps.

secondaryQueries: how to write a bug report
bug report fields jira azure devops

faq.q: What makes a good bug report?
faq.a: A good bug report lets someone who was not there reproduce the bug without asking you anything. It has a specific title, numbered steps with test data, separate expected and actual results, the exact environment and build, and evidence such as a screenshot, recording or log. It also says how often the bug happens.

faq.q: What is the difference between severity and priority?
faq.a: Severity describes how badly the defect affects the system; priority describes how soon the team should fix it. QA usually proposes severity from the technical impact, while priority is set during triage with the product owner, because it depends on business factors such as deadlines, affected users and available workarounds.

faq.q: What is the difference between a bug, a defect and an issue?
faq.a: In everyday QA use, bug and defect mean the same thing: the software does not meet its requirements or its expected behavior. Issue is broader. In trackers such as Jira, an issue (now often called a work item) is any tracked item, and Bug is one type, next to Task and Story.

faq.q: How long should a bug report title be?
faq.a: Short enough to read in a list view, usually one line: the area, what broke, and the condition. 'Checkout: total shows $0 after applying a coupon' works; 'Checkout bug' does not. Put details in the steps, not the title, and avoid words like 'broken' or 'doesn't work' that say nothing.

faq.q: Can you show an example of a good bug report?
faq.a: A good example: title 'Login: form submits with empty email, no validation error (Chrome)'; steps: open /login, leave both fields empty, click Sign in; expected: an 'Email is required' error and no request sent; actual: a spinner, then nothing; plus the browser, OS and build, a screen recording, and how often it happens.

body:
A good bug report lets a developer who was not there reproduce the bug on the first try. It has a specific title, numbered steps with the test data you used, separate expected and actual results, the exact environment, and evidence. Below is a complete bug report example, a template you can copy, and how the same fields map to Jira and Azure DevOps.

{/* [ADD YOUR EXPERIENCE: a short, anonymized story of a bug report that bounced back to you, or one you received, and the single missing detail that caused the back-and-forth. No employer, product or client names.] */}

<KeyTakeaways>
- Write for someone who has never seen your screen and has five minutes to investigate.
- One action per step, with the exact test data you used.
- Keep expected and actual results separate, and quote error messages exactly.
- Severity is impact, priority is urgency. Propose severity; let triage set priority.
- Attach evidence, and remove passwords, tokens and personal data from it first.
</KeyTakeaways>

## What does a good bug report example look like?

Here is a complete report for a real-world kind of defect: a form that should reject empty input but submits anyway, in one browser only. Every field answers a question the developer would otherwise have to ask.

<BugReport
  id="QA-1042"
  title="Login: form submits with an empty email field, no validation error (Chrome)"
  severity="high"
  priority="P2"
  status="open"
  environment="Chrome 158.0 | Windows 11 | Staging, build 2.4.1"
  reportedBy="Dipak Bist"
  assignedTo="Web team"
  preconditions="Signed out. Login page open at https://staging.example.com/login. Both fields empty."
  testData={`Email: (empty)\nPassword: (empty)`}
  steps={[
    "Open https://staging.example.com/login",
    "Leave the Email field empty",
    "Leave the Password field empty",
    "Click Sign in"
  ]}
  expected="An inline error, 'Email is required', appears under the Email field. No sign-in request is sent."
  actual="A sign-in request is sent (POST /api/session returns 400). A spinner shows for about 2 seconds, then disappears. No error message appears, and the user stays on the login page."
  attachments="Screen recording (12 seconds). Network tab export of the POST /api/session request and its response. Browser console: no errors."
  notes="Happens every time in Chrome (5 of 5 tries). Does not happen in Firefox 159.0, where the error shows correctly. Safari not tested."
/>

Why this example works:

- **The title names the area, the failure and the condition.** A developer scanning the backlog knows what it is without opening it.
- **The steps start from a known state.** The preconditions say signed out and which page, so nobody guesses the starting point.
- **Expected and actual are concrete.** The expected result quotes the message; the actual result includes what the network shows, not only what the screen shows.
- **The notes narrow it down.** "Every time in Chrome, never in Firefox" tells the developer where to look before they open the code.

## Which fields should every bug report include?

Every report needs enough for someone else to reproduce the bug, judge its impact, and later verify the fix. These fields cover that:

| Field | What to write | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Title | Area, what broke, and the condition | Checkout: total shows $0 after applying a coupon |
| Environment | Browser or app version, OS, test environment, build | Chrome 158.0, Windows 11, staging build 2.4.1 |
| Preconditions | The state before step 1 | Signed in as a customer with one item in the cart |
| Test data | The exact values you used | Coupon code SAVE10 |
| Steps | Numbered, one action each | 1. Open the cart. 2. Enter SAVE10. 3. Click Apply |
| Expected result | What the requirement says should happen | Total drops by 10% |
| Actual result | What happened, with exact messages | Total shows $0.00; no error |
| Frequency | Always, sometimes (how often), or once | 3 of 3 tries |
| Severity | Impact on the system | High |
| Priority | Proposed urgency, confirmed in triage | P2 |
| Evidence | Recording, screenshot, logs, network export | Screen recording attached |

## How do you write a bug report title?

Use the pattern **area: what broke + condition**. The title is the most-read part of the report, so it should make sense in a list view with nothing else around it.

**Weak titles:**
- "Login doesn't work"
- "Bug on checkout page"
- "App crashes"

**Strong titles:**
- "Login: form submits with empty email, no validation error (Chrome)"
- "Checkout: order total shows $0 after applying a coupon"
- "Reports: PDF export crashes on reports over 500 rows (Safari)"

## How do you write steps to reproduce?

Write one action per step, in order, from a known starting state, with the exact data you used. The last step is the one where the bug shows. If a step depends on something you did earlier, such as being signed in, move it into the preconditions.

**Weak steps:**
> Go to the cart and apply a coupon. Total is wrong.

**Strong steps:**
> 1. Sign in as `customer.qa@example.com`.
> 2. Add one "Basic plan" to the cart.
> 3. Open the cart.
> 4. Type `SAVE10` into the Coupon field and click **Apply**.

Before you submit, follow your own steps once more, exactly as written. If you cannot reproduce it from the text alone, neither can the developer.

## How do you write the expected and actual results?

State the expected result from the requirement, and the actual result as exactly as you can: quote messages word for word, and include what the network or console shows. Never write "it doesn't work": say what happened instead.

**Weak:**
> Expected: It works.
> Actual: It doesn't work.

**Strong:**
> Expected: Clicking **Place order** shows the toast "Order placed!" and opens `/orders/123` within 2 seconds.
> Actual: Clicking **Place order** shows a spinner for 10 seconds, then a blank page. No toast. The URL stays `/checkout`. `POST /api/orders` returns `500`.

For an API bug, paste the request (method, URL and body) and the response (status and body). If an automated test found it, its failure output is evidence too; see [how to test REST APIs with Playwright in Python](/blog/playwright-api-testing-guide).

## What is the difference between severity and priority?

Severity is how badly the defect affects the system; priority is how soon the team should fix it. They are set separately because they often disagree: a crash in a rarely used screen can be severe but not urgent, and a typo on the home page can be trivial but urgent.

| | Low priority | High priority |
|---|---|---|
| **High severity** | A rarely used admin export crashes, and a workaround exists | Checkout fails for every customer |
| **Low severity** | A typo on an internal settings page | The company name is misspelled on the home page |

Azure DevOps documents the same idea with an example: a rarely used link that crashes a page might get **Severity 2 - High** but **Priority 3**, because the experience is severe but rare ([Microsoft's guide to managing bugs in Azure Boards](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/boards/backlogs/manage-bugs?view=azure-devops)). Its four severity levels are a good default if your team has none:

| Severity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1 - Critical | A component or the whole system stops, or data is badly corrupted, and there is no workaround |
| 2 - High | The same impact as critical, but an acceptable workaround exists |
| 3 - Medium | The system gives incorrect, incomplete or inconsistent results |
| 4 - Low | A minor or cosmetic problem with an acceptable workaround |

## How do the fields map to Jira and Azure DevOps?

Both tools have a place for every field above, but the names differ, and Jira has no severity field out of the box.

| Bug report field | Jira | Azure DevOps (Bug work item) |
|---|---|---|
| Title | Summary | Title |
| Steps, expected and actual | Description | Repro Steps |
| Environment | Environment, if your project shows it; otherwise the description | System Info |
| Build or version | Affects versions, if your project uses versions | Found In Build |
| Severity | Not there by default: an admin adds it as a custom field | Severity (1 - Critical to 4 - Low) |
| Priority | Priority | Priority (1 is the highest) |
| Evidence | Attachments | Attachments |
| Fixed in | Fix versions | Integrated in Build |

Two notes on these tools:

- **Severity in Jira.** Jira Software projects do not include a Severity field by default, so teams usually add a single-select custom field. Sites that also use Jira Service Management may already have one ([Atlassian Community discussion](https://community.atlassian.com/forums/discussion/1117643/why-there-is-no-severity-field-for-issue-type-bug)).
- **Regressions in Azure DevOps.** Microsoft's guidance is not to reopen a closed bug when the problem comes back, but to open a new bug and link it to the old one with a Related link.

## What evidence should you attach?

Attach at least one piece of evidence, and pick the one that shows the problem fastest:

1. **A screen recording** for anything involving timing, animation or several steps.
2. **A screenshot** with the problem area marked.
3. **The browser console output**, copied in full, not just the first line.
4. **A network export** of the failing request: in DevTools, open the Network tab and save the request and its response.
5. **Server logs**, if you have access, with the timestamp of your test.

<Callout type="warning" title="Clean your evidence before you attach it">
  Screenshots, logs and network exports can contain passwords, session tokens, API keys and customer data. A browser network export (HAR file) includes cookies and authorization headers. Remove or mask them before you attach anything to a ticket.
</Callout>

## What are the most common bug report mistakes?

<QAChecklist
  title="Check before you submit"
  items={[
    { text: "The title names the area, what broke and the condition" },
    { text: "Steps are numbered, one action each, from a known starting state" },
    { text: "The test data you used is written down" },
    { text: "Expected and actual results are separate and concrete" },
    { text: "Error messages are quoted exactly" },
    { text: "Browser or app version, OS, environment and build are listed" },
    { text: "Frequency is stated: always, sometimes (how often), or once" },
    { text: "Evidence is attached, with secrets and personal data removed" },
    { text: "You searched for an existing report of the same bug" },
    { text: "You reproduced it once more by following your own steps" },
  ]}
/>

## Bug report template (copy-ready)

Copy this into Jira, Azure DevOps or GitHub Issues, and delete any line that does not apply.

```markdown title="bug-report-template.md"
## Title
[Area]: what broke + condition

## Environment
- Browser or app version:
- OS:
- Test environment and URL:
- Build or version:
- User role or account type:

## Severity: [ Critical | High | Medium | Low ]
## Priority (proposed): [ P1 | P2 | P3 | P4 ]

## Preconditions
The state before step 1.

## Test data
The exact values used.

## Steps to reproduce
1.
2.
3.

## Expected result
What the requirement or design says should happen.

## Actual result
What happens instead. Quote error messages exactly.

## Frequency
Always / Sometimes (x of y tries) / Once

## Evidence
- Recording:
- Screenshot:
- Console or network output:

## Notes
- Workaround:
- Other browsers or devices tried:
- Related tickets:
```

## How does a bug report become a regression test?

Once the bug is fixed, its steps and expected result are a ready-made test case: run them to verify the fix, then keep them in the regression suite so the bug cannot quietly return.

<TestCase
  id="REG-1042"
  title="Login rejects an empty email field"
  objective="Verify the fix for QA-1042 and guard against a regression"
  preconditions="Signed out, on /login, both fields empty"
  testData={`Email: (empty)\nPassword: (empty)`}
  steps={[
    { action: "Leave the Email field empty", expected: "The field stays empty" },
    { action: "Leave the Password field empty", expected: "The field stays empty" },
    { action: "Click Sign in", expected: "'Email is required' appears under the Email field and no sign-in request is sent" },
  ]}
  priority="high"
  type="Regression"
  author="Dipak Bist"
/>

A check like this runs on every release, so it is a good candidate for automation. To decide case by case, use this [checklist for when to automate a test](/blog/manual-vs-automation-testing).

## Can AI help you write better bug reports?

Yes, for spotting what is missing. An AI tool can point out a vague title, a missing environment or merged steps. It cannot know how your product should behave, so the expected result must come from the requirement, and it should never see real customer data, passwords or internal URLs.

<PromptBlock
  title="Review my bug report"
  context="You are a senior QA engineer who writes clear, precise bug reports."
  prompt={`Review this bug report draft:

Title: Login broken
Steps: Go to login page, click sign in
Expected: should work
Actual: doesn't work

Rewrite it with:
- A specific title: area, what broke, condition
- Numbered steps, one action each
- Separate expected and actual results
- A suggested severity, with your reason
- A list of the questions I must answer to fill in what is missing`}
  tip="Replace names, emails, tokens and internal URLs with placeholders before you paste a draft into any AI tool."
/>

For more on core QA skills, see all [QA fundamentals articles](/blog/category/qa-fundamentals).

title: When to Automate a Test: A Practical Checklist
description: When to automate a test and when not to: a 7-question checklist, a manual vs automation testing comparison, and a tested Playwright example to start with.
excerpt: Automate a test when it runs often, stays stable and has a result code can check. Keep it manual when it needs judgment. Seven yes-or-no questions make the call for any single test.

blogMeta.testedWith: Playwright for Python 1.65.1, pytest-playwright 0.10.0, pytest 9.2.0, Chromium 158.0.8127.18, Python 3.12.3

faq.q: Can automation testing completely replace manual testing?
faq.a: No. Automation checks what you already know to check: it repeats the same steps and compares results with fixed expectations. It cannot notice a confusing screen, a missing requirement or a risk nobody wrote a test for. Exploratory and usability testing need a person, so in practice the two are combined.

faq.q: Should I automate tests before the feature is stable?
faq.a: Usually not at the UI level. If the screens and flows still change every sprint, UI tests break for reasons that are not bugs, and maintenance eats the time they save. Automate at the API or unit level first, where contracts change less, and add UI automation once the flow is signed off.

faq.q: How do you decide what percentage of tests to automate?
faq.a: Don't start from a percentage. Decide test by test: automate the checks that run often, have stable steps and a clear expected result, and cost more to run by hand than to maintain. The percentage is an outcome of those decisions, and it differs between products, teams and test levels.

faq.q: Does the same checklist apply to API tests?
faq.a: Yes, and API tests usually pass it more easily. API contracts change less often than screens, the checks are precise, and the tests run fast without a browser. That is the idea behind the test pyramid: many fast API and unit tests, and fewer browser tests for the journeys only a browser can prove.

Skip automation for one-off checks, features that are about to change, tests that need human judgment such as usability or whether a design looks right, and flows you cannot make deterministic, such as real payment providers or CAPTCHAs. Exploratory testing also stays manual, because its value is in what the tester decides to try next.

body:
Automate a test when it runs often, its steps and expected result are stable, and running it by hand costs more than keeping the automation working. Keep it manual when it needs human judgment, runs once, or covers a feature that is still changing. The checklist below turns that into seven yes-or-no questions you can apply to any single test.

{/* [ADD YOUR EXPERIENCE: one sentence on how your team decides what to automate today, or the question that comes up most often when you plan automation. Keep it generic.] */}

<KeyTakeaways>
- Decide test by test, not with a target percentage.
- Automate checks that repeat, stay stable, and have a result code can verify.
- Keep exploratory, usability and one-off checks manual.
- Automate at the lowest level that can catch the bug: unit or API before the UI.
- Judge automation by the real bugs it catches, not by how many tests exist.
</KeyTakeaways>

## How do you decide whether to automate a test?

Answer these seven questions for the one test in front of you. The first three are must-haves; the rest decide when, and at which level, to automate.

<QAChecklist
  title="Should this test be automated?"
  items={[
    { text: "1. It will run many times: every build, every sprint, or before every release" },
    { text: "2. The same input gives the same result: no human judgment, no randomness" },
    { text: "3. Code can check the expected result: a value, a status, a message, an element" },
    { text: "4. The feature is stable: its flow is signed off and not being redesigned" },
    { text: "5. The test can create and clean up its own data" },
    { text: "6. Over the next few months, running it by hand costs more than building and maintaining it" },
    { text: "7. Someone on the team can fix it when it breaks" },
  ]}
/>

How to read the answers:

- **Yes to all seven:** automate it now.
- **No to question 1, 2 or 3:** keep it manual. Automation will not pay back, or it cannot check the result.
- **Yes to 1 to 3, but no to any of 4 to 7:** automate later, or at a lower level. An API test is often stable while the UI is not.

## How does the checklist work on real tests?

Here are three typical tests run through the checklist:

| Question | Sign in with valid credentials | "Is the new onboarding flow easy to follow?" | Monthly invoice PDF |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Runs many times | Yes: every build | Yes: every design change | No: once a month |
| 2. Same input, same result | Yes | No: it is a judgment | Yes for the numbers |
| 3. Code can check the result | Yes: the URL and heading | No | The totals yes, the look no |
| 4. Stable feature | Yes | No: still in design | Yes |
| 5. Creates its own data | Yes: a test account | Not relevant | Yes |
| 6. Cheaper automated | Yes | No | For the totals |
| 7. Someone can maintain it | Yes | Not relevant | Yes |
| **Decision** | **Automate as a UI smoke test** | **Keep manual: usability** | **Automate the totals at API level; check the layout by hand** |

The third column is the common case: one feature, two decisions. Split the test along the line between what code can check and what needs a person.

{/* [ADD YOUR EXPERIENCE: one test from your own work that you decided not to automate, and the checklist question that decided it. Keep it generic.] */}

## What should not be automated?

Keep these manual, or automate only the part that code can check:

- **Exploratory testing.** Its value is in what the tester decides to try next. Write a charter, not a script.
- **Usability, and look and feel.** Code can check that a button exists, not whether people understand it. Visual regression tools catch changes, but a person still decides whether a change is right.
- **One-off checks.** A data migration you run once does not repay the effort of automating it.
- **Features that are still changing.** UI tests written now break with every redesign, for reasons that are not bugs.
- **Flows you cannot make deterministic.** Real payment providers, CAPTCHAs and third-party emails. Test your side of them with stubs at the API level instead.
- **Accessibility, beyond the basics.** Automated scanners catch some problems, such as missing alt text or low contrast, but not whether a screen reader user can finish the task.

The Ministry of Testing community has a long thread on [what should not be automated](https://club.ministryoftesting.com/t/what-should-not-be-automated/43058), with examples from many teams.

## Manual vs automation testing: how do they compare?

Manual testing is a person running the test and judging the result. Automation testing is code running the test and comparing the result with fixed expectations. Each is strong where the other is weak:

| | Manual testing | Automation testing |
|---|---|---|
| Best at | New features, exploring, usability, one-off checks | Regression, smoke tests, many data combinations |
| Finds | New and unexpected problems | Regressions in behavior that is already checked |
| Cost to start | Low | High: writing and debugging the tests |
| Cost to repeat | The same effort every run | Low per run, plus maintenance when the product changes |
| Speed per run | Slow | Fast once built |
| Judgment | Yes | None: only what the code asserts |
| Consistency | Varies between runs and testers | The same steps every run |
| Runs in CI | No | Yes |

## Where should automated tests sit?

As low in the stack as the check allows. The test pyramid describes the balance: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration and API tests in the middle, and the fewest end-to-end UI tests at the top, because UI tests are the slowest and break most easily. Martin Fowler's [Practical Test Pyramid](https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html) explains it with examples, and Google's testing blog argues the same point in [Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests](https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/04/just-say-no-to-more-end-to-end-tests.html).

In practice:

- **Unit tests**, usually written by developers, check logic and edge cases.
- **API tests** check business rules, permissions and data without a browser. See [how to write Playwright API tests in Python](/blog/playwright-api-testing-guide).
- **UI tests** check the few journeys that only make sense in a browser, such as signing in or checking out.

## What is a good first test to automate?

Signing in with valid credentials passes all seven questions, which makes it a common first UI test. Here it is in Playwright for Python, with its negative twin:

```python title="tests/test_login.py"
import re

from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect


def test_login_with_valid_credentials(page: Page):
    page.goto("/login")

    page.get_by_label("Email").fill("qa.user@example.com")
    page.get_by_label("Password").fill("correct-horse-battery")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()

    expect(page).to_have_url(re.compile(r"/dashboard$"))
    expect(page.get_by_role("heading", level=1)).to_have_text("Welcome, QA User")


def test_login_with_wrong_password_shows_an_error(page: Page):
    page.goto("/login")

    page.get_by_label("Email").fill("qa.user@example.com")
    page.get_by_label("Password").fill("wrong-password")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()

    expect(page.get_by_role("alert")).to_have_text("Email or password is incorrect.")
    expect(page).to_have_url(re.compile(r"/login$"))
```

Three things make this test hold up:

- **The locators are what a user sees:** a label, a button name, a heading. They survive markup changes better than CSS selectors; see [Playwright's guide to locators](https://playwright.dev/python/docs/locators).
- **`expect` waits.** Each assertion retries until it passes or times out, so there are no `sleep()` calls. See [Playwright's assertions](https://playwright.dev/python/docs/test-assertions).
- **`page.goto("/login")` is relative.** pytest-playwright passes the `base_url` fixture to every browser context, so the app's address lives in one place.

The tests run against a small local login app that starts with the test session, so they run anywhere. The [login test example project on GitHub](https://github.com/DipakBist08/myportfolio/tree/main/blog/examples/manual-vs-automation-testing) has the app and its `conftest.py`. This is the run for this article:

```text
tests/test_login.py::test_login_with_valid_credentials[chromium] PASSED  [ 50%]
tests/test_login.py::test_login_with_wrong_password_shows_an_error[chromium] PASSED [100%]

============================== 2 passed in 1.21s ===============================
```

Now compare what a manual tester notices on the same screen: an error message that confuses people, a password field that hides the Caps Lock warning, a layout that breaks on a small phone. Neither kind of testing replaces the other.

## How do you know if your test automation is working?

Measure what it catches and what it costs, not how many tests exist:

- **Real bugs caught before release.** If the suite has not caught one in months, it may be checking the wrong things.
- **False failures.** How often does a red build turn out to be a flaky or outdated test? Each one costs a person's time and the team's trust.
- **Run time.** A suite that takes too long stops being run on every change.

A team with 2,000 tests that never catch anything gets less from automation than a team with 50 well-chosen tests that catch real regressions.

## What are the most common automation mistakes?

- **Automating too early.** UI tests for a feature still in design break every sprint. Wait until the flow is signed off, or test the API first.
- **Automating a flaky flow without fixing it.** Flaky tests teach the team to ignore red builds. Fix the test isolation or the timing first.
- **Dropping manual testing entirely.** Automation only checks what you already thought of. Keep exploratory sessions for new features.
- **Putting every check in the UI.** Checks that could run as API tests take longer and break more often as UI tests.
- **Counting tests instead of results.** See the previous section.

When an automated check does catch a real bug, report it so it gets fixed fast; this [bug report example](/blog/how-to-write-good-bug-report) shows what to include.

For more on test strategy and core QA skills, see all [QA fundamentals articles](/blog/category/qa-fundamentals).

title: Playwright API Testing in Python, No Browser Needed
description: Playwright API testing in Python with pytest: CRUD requests, JSON Schema checks, 401 and 403 cases, negative tests and CI. All 25 tests were run and pass.
excerpt: Playwright's request API tests REST endpoints from Python without launching a browser. This guide builds a small pytest suite step by step, and every test in it runs and passes.

blogMeta.testedWith: Playwright for Python 1.65.1, pytest-playwright 0.10.0, pytest 9.2.0, jsonschema 4.26.0, Python 3.12.3

faq.q: Is Playwright good for API testing without a browser?
faq.a: Yes. Playwright's APIRequestContext sends HTTP requests directly, so API tests never launch a browser. The example suite in this guide passed with no browser binaries installed at all. It is a good fit when your team already uses Playwright for UI tests and wants one tool, one set of fixtures, and shared login state.

faq.q: How do I share authentication tokens across Playwright API tests?
faq.a: Create the request context once, in a session-scoped pytest fixture, and pass the token in extra_http_headers. Every test that uses the fixture then sends the same Authorization header. Read the token from an environment variable, not from the code, so it never gets committed to Git or shared by accident.

faq.q: Can I use Playwright API tests and browser tests in the same project?
faq.a: Yes. pytest-playwright gives you both the page fixture for browser tests and the playwright fixture for API contexts, in the same suite. A common pattern is to create test data through the API, then check it in the UI. Storage state can also move between API and browser contexts.

faq.q: How do I send a POST request with Playwright in Python?
faq.a: Call post() on an APIRequestContext with the path and a dict in the data argument, for example api_context.post('/users', data=payload). Playwright serializes a dict to JSON and sets the Content-Type header to application/json for you. Use form= for form-encoded bodies and multipart= for file uploads.

body:
Playwright API testing in Python means sending HTTP requests through Playwright's `APIRequestContext` and checking the responses with pytest, without opening a browser. You get Playwright's fixtures, assertions and auth handling for your API layer, in the same project as your UI tests. This guide builds a complete test suite step by step, and every test in it was run and passes.

{/* [ADD YOUR EXPERIENCE: one or two sentences on where Playwright API tests helped you at work, for example creating test data before a UI test, or catching a broken endpoint before the UI did. Keep it generic: no employer, product or client names.] */}

<KeyTakeaways>
- `APIRequestContext` sends HTTP requests directly. The suite in this guide passes with no browsers installed.
- Create the request context once per test session, with the base URL and the auth header.
- For every write, check the status, the body and the stored data. A `201` alone proves little.
- `jsonschema` ignores `"format"` rules such as email unless you pass a `FormatChecker`.
- Test `401`, `403` and bad input as carefully as the happy path.
</KeyTakeaways>

## What do you need for Playwright API testing in Python?

You need Python 3.10 or newer and two packages: `pytest-playwright`, which installs Playwright and pytest, and `jsonschema` for response validation. You do not need to run `playwright install`, because API tests never start a browser.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # on Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install pytest-playwright jsonschema
```

These are the exact versions this guide was tested with:

```text title="requirements.txt"
playwright==1.65.1
pytest==9.2.0
pytest-playwright==0.10.0
jsonschema==4.26.0
```

<Callout type="info" title="No browser download needed">
  `pip install playwright` installs the library and its driver, not the browsers. Browsers come from the separate `playwright install` step, which API-only suites can skip. The example suite for this guide passes with Playwright pointed at an empty browser folder (`PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH`), so no browser is involved at any point.
</Callout>

## What API will the tests run against?

The examples test a small users API. So that every example runs for anyone, with no account and no network access, the example project includes a mock of that API: `mock_api.py`, written with the Python standard library only. It starts on a free local port when the test session starts. To point the same tests at another API, set `API_BASE_URL`.

| Request | Success | Expected errors |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /users/{id}` | `200` with the user | `401`, `404` |
| `POST /users` | `201` with the new user | `400` missing field, `422` invalid value, `409` email taken, `401`, `403` |
| `PATCH /users/{id}` | `200` with the updated user | `422` invalid value, `404`, `401`, `403` |
| `DELETE /users/{id}` | `204` with no body | `404`, `401`, `403` |
| `GET /admin/settings` | `200` | `401`, `403` |

There are two tokens: `admin-token` can read and write, and `viewer-token` can only read. The complete project, with the mock and all 25 tests, is in the [Playwright API testing example project on GitHub](https://github.com/DipakBist08/myportfolio/tree/main/blog/examples/playwright-api-testing-guide).

## How do you set up an APIRequestContext with pytest?

Create one `APIRequestContext` per test session in `conftest.py`, with the base URL and the headers every request needs. pytest-playwright provides the `playwright` fixture you build it from. Dispose of the context at the end of the session to free its memory.

```python title="conftest.py"
import os
import uuid
from typing import Iterator

import pytest
from playwright.sync_api import APIRequestContext, Playwright

import mock_api


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def base_url() -> Iterator[str]:
    """Use API_BASE_URL when it is set; otherwise start the local mock API."""
    external = os.environ.get("API_BASE_URL")
    if external:  # an empty value (an unset CI variable) falls through to the mock
        yield external
        return
    server, url = mock_api.start()
    yield url
    server.shutdown()


def new_context(playwright: Playwright, base_url: str, token: str | None) -> APIRequestContext:
    headers = {"Accept": "application/json"}
    if token:
        headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"
    return playwright.request.new_context(base_url=base_url, extra_http_headers=headers)


def token(name: str, mock_default: str) -> str:
    # `or`, not a get() default: CI sets the variable to "" when a secret is missing.
    return os.environ.get(name) or mock_default


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def api_context(playwright: Playwright, base_url: str) -> Iterator[APIRequestContext]:
    """Requests sent as an admin. The token comes from the environment, never from the code."""
    context = new_context(playwright, base_url, token("API_TOKEN", "admin-token"))
    yield context
    context.dispose()


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def viewer_context(playwright: Playwright, base_url: str) -> Iterator[APIRequestContext]:
    """Requests sent as a read-only user."""
    context = new_context(playwright, base_url, token("API_VIEWER_TOKEN", "viewer-token"))
    yield context
    context.dispose()


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def anonymous_context(playwright: Playwright, base_url: str) -> Iterator[APIRequestContext]:
    """Requests sent with no token at all."""
    context = new_context(playwright, base_url, token=None)
    yield context
    context.dispose()


@pytest.fixture
def unique_email() -> str:
    """A fresh address per test, so tests never collide on the unique-email rule."""
    return f"qa-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}@example.com"


@pytest.fixture
def created_user(api_context: APIRequestContext, unique_email: str) -> Iterator[dict]:
    """Create a user for one test and delete it afterwards, even if the test fails."""
    response = api_context.post("/users", data={"name": "QA Tester", "email": unique_email, "role": "viewer"})
    assert response.status == 201, response.text()
    user = response.json()
    yield user
    api_context.delete(f"/users/{user['id']}")  # 404 is fine if the test already deleted it
```

Three details in this file prevent common problems:

- **The token comes from the environment.** `API_TOKEN` is read with `or` instead of a `get()` default, because CI systems pass a missing secret as an empty string.
- **Every test gets its own email address.** `unique_email` stops tests from colliding on the "email must be unique" rule, so they can run in any order, or twice in a row.
- **Test data is cleaned up.** `created_user` deletes the user after the test, even when the test fails, because pytest runs fixture teardown either way.

Official references: [API testing in the Playwright for Python docs](https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api-testing) and [how pytest fixtures work](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/fixtures.html).

## How do you test a GET request?

Send the request, check the status, then check the body. `expect(response).to_be_ok()` passes for any status from 200 to 299, so compare `response.status` directly when the exact code matters, as in the 404 test below.

```python title="tests/test_users_read.py"
from playwright.sync_api import APIRequestContext, expect


def test_get_user_returns_the_user(api_context: APIRequestContext):
    response = api_context.get("/users/1")

    expect(response).to_be_ok()  # any 2xx status

    body = response.json()
    assert body["id"] == 1
    assert body["email"] == "asha@example.com"
    assert response.headers["content-type"] == "application/json"


def test_get_missing_user_returns_404(api_context: APIRequestContext):
    response = api_context.get("/users/999999")

    assert response.status == 404
    assert response.json() == {"error": "not_found"}


def test_list_users_includes_a_created_user(api_context: APIRequestContext, created_user: dict):
    response = api_context.get("/users")

    expect(response).to_be_ok()
    assert created_user["id"] in [user["id"] for user in response.json()]
```

This is the response the first test checks:

<APIRequest
  method="GET"
  url="/users/1"
  headers={{ "Authorization": "Bearer <token>", "Accept": "application/json" }}
  status={200}
  response={`{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Asha Rai",
  "email": "asha@example.com",
  "role": "admin"
}`}
  description="Response from the example project's mock API."
/>

The assertion is documented in the [APIResponseAssertions reference](https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api/class-apiresponseassertions).

## How do you test POST, PATCH and DELETE requests?

For every write, check three things: the status code, the response body, and the stored data, by reading the record back. An API can answer `201` or `200` and still fail to save the change, and only the read-back catches that.

Written as a manual test case, the flow looks like this. The tests below automate each step.

<TestCase
  id="API-001"
  title="Create, update and delete a user through the REST API"
  objective="The users API stores changes and removes deleted users"
  preconditions="An admin token. The email address used is not taken."
  testData={`name: QA Tester\nemail: a new, unique address\nrole: viewer`}
  type="API"
  priority="high"
  author="Dipak Bist"
  steps={[
    { action: "POST /users with the test data", expected: "201, and the body echoes the name, email and role with a numeric id" },
    { action: "PATCH /users/{id} with a new email", expected: "200, and GET /users/{id} returns the new email" },
    { action: "DELETE /users/{id}", expected: "204 with no body" },
    { action: "GET /users/{id}", expected: "404: the user is gone" },
  ]}
/>

```python title="tests/test_users_write.py"
from playwright.sync_api import APIRequestContext, expect


def test_create_user(api_context: APIRequestContext, unique_email: str):
    payload = {"name": "QA Tester", "email": unique_email, "role": "viewer"}

    response = api_context.post("/users", data=payload)  # a dict is sent as JSON

    assert response.status == 201
    body = response.json()
    assert isinstance(body["id"], int)
    assert {key: body[key] for key in payload} == payload

    api_context.delete(f"/users/{body['id']}")  # clean up what this test created


def test_update_user_email(api_context: APIRequestContext, created_user: dict, unique_email: str):
    new_email = f"updated-{unique_email}"

    response = api_context.patch(f"/users/{created_user['id']}", data={"email": new_email})

    expect(response).to_be_ok()
    assert response.json()["email"] == new_email
    # Read it back: the update must be stored, not only echoed in the response.
    assert api_context.get(f"/users/{created_user['id']}").json()["email"] == new_email


def test_delete_user(api_context: APIRequestContext, created_user: dict):
    user_url = f"/users/{created_user['id']}"

    delete_response = api_context.delete(user_url)
    assert delete_response.status == 204

    assert api_context.get(user_url).status == 404  # it is really gone
    assert api_context.delete(user_url).status == 404  # deleting twice is not a success
```

Two details worth copying:

- **`data=` with a dict is sent as JSON.** Playwright also sets `Content-Type: application/json` for you. Use `form=` for form-encoded bodies and `multipart=` for file uploads. See the [APIRequestContext reference](https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext).
- **The delete test deletes twice.** In this API's contract the second call returns `404`. Some APIs return `204` again by design. Whichever your API documents, test it, so a change in behavior gets noticed.

## How do you validate an API response with JSON Schema?

Describe the expected shape of a response once, as a JSON Schema, and validate responses against it. Schema checks catch a renamed field, a wrong type or an unexpected extra field, which checks on one or two values miss.

```python title="tests/test_schema.py"
import pytest
from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator, FormatChecker, ValidationError
from playwright.sync_api import APIRequestContext

USER_SCHEMA = {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["id", "name", "email", "role"],
    "properties": {
        "id": {"type": "integer"},
        "name": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
        "email": {"type": "string", "format": "email"},
        "role": {"type": "string", "enum": ["admin", "editor", "viewer"]},
    },
    # Fail when the API starts returning a field nobody agreed on.
    "additionalProperties": False,
}

# "format" is only checked when a FormatChecker is passed in.
validator = Draft202012Validator(USER_SCHEMA, format_checker=FormatChecker())


def test_user_response_matches_schema(api_context: APIRequestContext):
    body = api_context.get("/users/1").json()

    validator.validate(body)  # raises ValidationError on a mismatch


def test_every_listed_user_matches_schema(api_context: APIRequestContext):
    for user in api_context.get("/users").json():
        validator.validate(user)


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "broken_user",
    [
        {"id": "1", "name": "Asha Rai", "email": "asha@example.com", "role": "admin"},  # id is a string
        {"id": 1, "name": "Asha Rai", "email": "not-an-email", "role": "admin"},  # bad email format
        {"id": 1, "name": "Asha Rai", "email": "asha@example.com", "role": "owner"},  # unknown role
        {"id": 1, "name": "Asha Rai", "email": "asha@example.com"},  # role is missing
        {"id": 1, "name": "Asha Rai", "email": "asha@example.com", "role": "admin", "password": "x"},  # extra field
    ],
)
def test_schema_rejects_a_broken_user(broken_user: dict):
    """Prove the schema can fail. A schema that accepts everything protects nothing."""
    with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
        validator.validate(broken_user)
```

`"additionalProperties": False` matters most for fields that should never leave the server, such as a password hash: the extra-field case in the last test is exactly that bug.

<Callout type="warning" title="Formats are not checked unless you ask">
  In the `jsonschema` library, `"format": "email"` is only an annotation by default, so `not-an-email` passes. Pass `format_checker=FormatChecker()` to enforce formats, as above. See [validating formats in the jsonschema docs](https://python-jsonschema.readthedocs.io/en/stable/validate/).
</Callout>

## How do you test 401 and 403 responses?

Test both failure modes. `401 Unauthorized` means the request has no valid credentials, and `403 Forbidden` means the credentials are valid but not allowed to do this (MDN: [401 Unauthorized](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/401), [403 Forbidden](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403)). Give each role its own request context, so every test shows who is calling.

```python title="tests/test_auth.py"
from playwright.sync_api import APIRequestContext, Playwright


def test_401_without_a_token(anonymous_context: APIRequestContext):
    response = anonymous_context.get("/users/1")

    assert response.status == 401
    assert response.json() == {"error": "unauthorized"}


def test_401_with_an_invalid_token(playwright: Playwright, base_url: str):
    context = playwright.request.new_context(
        base_url=base_url,
        extra_http_headers={"Authorization": "Bearer not-a-real-token"},
    )
    try:
        assert context.get("/users/1").status == 401
    finally:
        context.dispose()


def test_viewer_can_read(viewer_context: APIRequestContext):
    assert viewer_context.get("/users/1").status == 200


def test_403_when_a_viewer_opens_an_admin_endpoint(viewer_context: APIRequestContext):
    response = viewer_context.get("/admin/settings")

    assert response.status == 403
    assert response.json() == {"error": "forbidden"}


def test_403_when_a_viewer_tries_to_write(viewer_context: APIRequestContext, api_context: APIRequestContext, unique_email: str):
    response = viewer_context.post("/users", data={"name": "Should Not Exist", "email": unique_email})

    assert response.status == 403
    # The status code alone is not enough: check that nothing was created.
    assert unique_email not in [user["email"] for user in api_context.get("/users").json()]
```

The last test is the one many suites skip: it checks that the viewer's rejected request created nothing. A `403` with a side effect is still a security bug.

## How do you write negative API tests?

List the invalid inputs in a parametrize table, one row per case, with the expected status and the field the error should name. For each row, check three things: the status, the error body, and that nothing was created.

```python title="tests/test_negative.py"
import pytest
from playwright.sync_api import APIRequestContext


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "payload, expected_status, expected_fields",
    [
        pytest.param({}, 400, ["name", "email"], id="empty body"),
        pytest.param({"name": "No Email"}, 400, ["email"], id="email missing"),
        pytest.param({"name": "", "email": "a@example.com"}, 422, ["name"], id="name empty"),
        pytest.param({"name": "x" * 101, "email": "a@example.com"}, 422, ["name"], id="name too long"),
        pytest.param({"name": "Bad Email", "email": "not-an-email"}, 422, ["email"], id="email invalid"),
        pytest.param({"name": "Bad Role", "email": "a@example.com", "role": "owner"}, 422, ["role"], id="role unknown"),
    ],
)
def test_create_user_rejects_bad_input(api_context: APIRequestContext, payload, expected_status, expected_fields):
    users_before = len(api_context.get("/users").json())

    response = api_context.post("/users", data=payload)

    assert response.status == expected_status
    assert response.json()["fields"] == expected_fields  # the error says which fields are wrong
    assert len(api_context.get("/users").json()) == users_before  # and nothing was created


def test_create_user_rejects_a_duplicate_email(api_context: APIRequestContext, created_user: dict):
    response = api_context.post("/users", data={"name": "Twin", "email": created_user["email"]})

    assert response.status == 409
    assert response.json() == {"error": "email_taken"}
```

The split between `400` and `422` is this API's contract. Your API may use `400` for every validation error: test what your API documents, not these numbers. The `id=` labels make each case readable in the test report; see [parametrizing tests](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/parametrize.html) in the pytest docs.

Run pytest from the project folder:

```bash

```

## How do you run Playwright API tests in CI?

Install the requirements and run pytest. There is no `playwright install` step, because API tests need no browser. Store the token as a repository secret and pass it to the test step as an environment variable.

```yaml title=".github/workflows/api-tests.yml"
name: API tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  api-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - name: Run API tests
        run: pytest -v
        env:
          API_BASE_URL: ${{ vars.API_BASE_URL }}
          API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
```

When `API_BASE_URL` is not set, the tests start the mock API, so the workflow also runs in a fork that has no secrets.

## What are the most common mistakes in Playwright API tests?

- **A token hardcoded in `conftest.py`.** It ends up in Git history. Read it from an environment variable.
- **Checking only the status code.** Check the body too and, for writes, read the data back.
- **Fixed test data.** A test that always creates `qa@example.com` collides with itself on the second run. Generate unique values.
- **No cleanup.** Shared test environments fill up with leftover records. Delete what each test creates, in a fixture.
- **Returning a value from a test so a later test can use it.** pytest 9 warns with `PytestReturnNotNoneWarning`, and no other test can read the value. Share data through fixtures instead.
- **Trusting `"format"` in a schema without a `FormatChecker`.** The check silently does nothing.

## Can AI help you write API test cases?

AI tools are useful for a first list of cases, such as boundaries and missing fields. The model does not know your API's contract, so check every case against the documentation before you automate it, and never paste real tokens or customer data into the prompt.

<PromptBlock
  title="Draft API test cases"
  context="You are a senior QA engineer who specializes in API testing."
  prompt={`Here is an endpoint:
Method: POST
URL: /api/v1/orders
Body: { "product_id": int, "quantity": int, "user_id": int }
Rules: quantity is 1 to 100; product_id must exist.

List test cases for:
1. The happy path
2. Boundary values for quantity (0, 1, 100, 101)
3. Missing required fields
4. Wrong data types
5. No token, and a token without permission
6. The same request sent twice

Format: | ID | Description | Input | Expected status | Expected response |`}
  tip="Give the model your real business rules. Without them it guesses limits and status codes."
/>

## Where do API tests fit next to UI tests?

API tests run fast and fail with a precise message, so they can carry most functional checks, with fewer browser tests for the journeys only a browser can prove. For deciding which checks to automate at all, see [when to automate a test](/blog/manual-vs-automation-testing). When an API test does find a defect, report it with the exact request and response: this [bug report example](/blog/how-to-write-good-bug-report) shows the fields developers need.

For more on this topic, see all [API testing articles](/blog/category/api-testing).
